aspects.says: A full fence between a thread's write and its read rules out both reads missing the other thread's write.
basis: section:Acquire/Release Orders a Handoff, Not a Write Followed by a Read

aspects.says: If each thread keeps its program order, two threads that each write their own flag and then read the other's can't both read the old value; any interleaving lets at least one see the other's write.
basis: section:A Thread Keeps Its Own Order; Another Thread May See Its Accesses Reordered

aspects.says: The JIT reorders plain stores to different fields, so message passing through plain fields fails on x86 even though the hardware keeps stores in order; -Xint and C1 hid it.
basis: section:The JIT Reorders Too, So x86 Shows a Reordering Its Hardware Doesn't Make

aspects.says: Whether a given run shows a reordering depends on timing, hardware and JIT state.
basis: section:A Tool That Makes Two Threads Collide on Every Trial
aspects.reason: a reordering that shows only sometimes can't be graded deterministically; the page shows the counts and the quiz checks the reasoning

aspects.says: A reference read through a race may expose an object before its constructor's plain writes; not observed in these runs, but allowed by the JLS, so publish through volatile, a lock or final fields.
basis: section:A Racy Reference May Expose an Object Before Its Constructor's Writes Land

aspects.says: setRelease/getAcquire order a handoff but don't stop a read from overtaking the same thread's earlier release write; store buffering needs volatile or a full fence.
basis: section:Acquire/Release Orders a Handoff, Not a Write Followed by a Read

aspects.says: Intra-thread semantics lets the compiler and processor reorder accesses to different variables, because the thread itself can't tell; another thread can.
basis: section:A Thread Keeps Its Own Order; Another Thread May See Its Accesses Reordered

aspects.says: A store waits in the core's store buffer, so a later load can complete first as seen by other cores, while the thread's own loads read its buffered writes; on x86 the buffer drains in order.
basis: section:The Processor's Store Buffer Lets a Read Overtake an Earlier Write, with No JIT at All

aspects.says: volatile rules out both reorderings, but a write-then-read handshake needs both fields volatile; one volatile field is enough only for a handoff.
basis: section:volatile on Every Access That Needs Ordering Rules Out Both Reorderings
section:Spot the Problem: One Volatile Flag Out of Two
